Epidermis.description: The epidermis is the outer layer of the skin. In thick skin of the palms and soles it has five layers, from the basal layer where new cells are made up to the dead, flattened stratum corneum at the surface.
clinical: A callus is a local thickening of the stratum corneum that forms in response to repeated friction and pressure. Calluses are common on the palms and soles.

Epidermal cells.description: Keratinocytes are the cells that make up most of the epidermis. They are born in the basal layer, move upward through the spinous and granular layers, and at the surface have lost their nuclei and become flat, dead cells filled with keratin.
clinical: In psoriasis, keratinocytes turn over far faster than normal, so the epidermis thickens into raised, scaly plaques. Palms and soles can be affected.

Epidermal detail.description: Close-up detail inside the epidermal layers. Keratinocyte nuclei and keratohyalin granules mark the living layers, and cell borders outline the flattened dead cells at the surface. Melanocytes, the pigment cells of the basal layer, send dendrites between keratinocytes and pass them melanin in packets called melanosomes.
clinical: Acral melanoma is a melanoma that arises from melanocytes on the palms, soles and under the nails.
Stretch marks (striae) form when rapid stretching, as in growth or pregnancy, tears the collagen and elastic fibres of the dermis.

Hypodermis.description: The hypodermis, also called the subcutis, is the layer of fat under the dermis. Its fat lobules are separated by fibrous septa that anchor the dermis to deeper fascia and carry larger vessels and nerves. It insulates, cushions and stores energy.
clinical: Cellulitis is a bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous fat, making an area of skin red, warm, swollen and tender.

Vessels & nerves.description: Blood reaches the skin through arterioles, which feed the subpapillary plexus and a capillary loop in each dermal papilla, and venules drain it into the venous plexuses. Cutaneous nerves carry sensory fibres through the dermis, and free nerve endings in the epidermis and dermis detect pain, temperature and itch.

clinical: In cystic fibrosis a faulty CFTR chloride channel in the sweat duct stops chloride being reabsorbed, so sweat is unusually salty. This is the basis of the sweat chloride test.
Hyperhidrosis is excessive sweating, often focal and most common on the palms, soles and armpits. It is driven by overactive sympathetic stimulation of eccrine sweat glands.

Eccrine cellular detail.description: A close-up of the cells of an eccrine sweat gland. Clear cells make the watery primary sweat, dark cells add glycoprotein, and myoepithelial cells beneath them contract to push sweat out. The duct cells reabsorb salt, so sweat reaching the surface is less salty than the sweat made in the coil.

Sensory receptors.description: Specialised endings in the skin that detect touch and pressure. Meissner corpuscles, in the dermal papillae of hairless palm and sole skin, detect light touch and fine texture. Pacinian corpuscles are large, onion-like capsules of many concentric lamellae in the deep dermis and hypodermis, and they respond best to rapid vibration and changes in pressure.

Sensory cellular detail.description: A close-up of one Meissner corpuscle, a light-touch receptor in the dermal papillae of hairless palm and sole skin. Its capsule is made of flattened lamellar cells, which are modified Schwann cells, and the axon terminal inside them detects touch.

Closed covers.description: These are helper pieces that hide or reveal the surrounding tissue, so that each close-up cutaway can be seen. They are not body structures and have no teaching content of their own.

parts.description: The stratum corneum is the outermost layer of the epidermis, made of many layers of flattened, dead, nucleus-free cells called corneocytes packed with keratin. On the palms and soles it is very thick, and its surface is raised into friction ridges, the fingerprint pattern that improves grip, with sweat pores opening along the top of each ridge. It forms a tough, waterproof barrier that resists abrasion and limits water loss; in a section it appears as a pale, compact band at the surface.

The stratum corneum is the horny outer zone of the epidermis, the layer that meets the air. Its flattened, dead, nucleus-free cells (corneocytes) are filled with keratin and set in a lipid-rich matrix that makes the barrier waterproof. Cells are shed continuously from the surface in a process called desquamation (shedding), so the outer layer is always being renewed. In histological sections it is the pink, compact band that tops the epidermis.

The stratum lucidum (clear layer) is a thin, glassy band lying between the stratum granulosum and the stratum corneum, found only in the thick skin of the palms and soles. Its flattened cells have lost their nuclei and organelles and are packed with eleidin, a translucent substance that forms as an intermediate stage between keratohyalin granules and keratin. In haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) sections it appears as a sharply defined, pink (eosinophilic) band just above the dark granular cells.

In the epidermis of the palm and sole, the stratum lucidum is the translucent band of flattened, dead keratinocytes lying just beneath the stratum corneum. Its cells have lost their nuclei and organelles and contain eleidin, which gives them a glassy look under the microscope. Because it is absent from thin skin, its presence is a quick clue that a section comes from thick palmar or plantar skin.

The stratum granulosum (granular layer) is a band of flattened cells just below the stratum corneum, one to three layers thick in thin skin and three to five in thick skin. Its cells contain dark, blue-staining (basophilic) keratohyalin granules made of profilaggrin and loricrin, which give the layer its name. Lamellar bodies release lipid between cells to seal the waterproof barrier, and tight junctions form here before the nuclei and organelles break down. Loss-of-function mutations in the filaggrin gene cause ichthyosis vulgaris, a dry, scaly skin condition.

Lying between the living spinous cells and the dead surface layer, the stratum granulosum is a thin band of cells packed with dark keratohyalin granules, which make it a dark stripe in routinely stained sections. The granules contain profilaggrin, which is broken down into filaggrin to bundle keratin filaments together, and loricrin, a major protein of the tough cell envelope. Lipid-filled lamellar bodies are secreted here, and the nuclei and organelles are destroyed as the cells head towards the surface.

The stratum spinosum (prickle-cell layer) is the thickest living layer of the epidermis, made of several layers of many-sided (polyhedral) keratinocytes. Neighbouring cells are joined by many desmosomes, which look like small spines or prickles after fixation shrinks the cells, and the cells are rich in keratin filaments (K1 and K10). Langerhans cells, immune cells that present antigens, are scattered here. In pemphigus vulgaris, an autoimmune blistering disease, antibodies against desmoglein 3 split this layer just above the basal cells.

The stratum spinosum sits above the basal layer and forms a broad band of several cell layers that gives the epidermis much of its bulk. Its many-sided cells are linked by desmosomes, tiny anchoring junctions that look like short spines between cells in a section. The cells make K1 and K10 keratin filaments that give the epidermis its toughness, and Langerhans cells, antigen-presenting immune cells, lie among them.

The stratum basale (basal layer, or stratum germinativum) is the single row of cuboidal to columnar cells that rests directly on the basement membrane, the boundary with the dermis. These stem and dividing keratinocytes express K5 and K14 and are anchored by hemidesmosomes, attachments that bind them to the membrane and are the target of bullous pemphigoid. Its undersurface forms the rete ridges that interlock with the dermal papillae. Melanocytes (about one in ten basal cells) and Merkel cells, touch receptors, also lie here.

The stratum basale is the deepest row of the epidermis, sitting on the basement membrane that separates it from the dermis. Its cells keep the epidermis supplied with new keratinocytes, dividing to replace those shed from the surface. Each cell is tied to the membrane by hemidesmosomes, and the basal layer is also home to melanocytes and Merkel cells. In a section, look for a single row of small, darkly stained nuclei along the dermal border.

The papillary dermis is the thin upper layer of the dermis, lying directly beneath the epidermis and filling the dermal papillae, the finger-like projections that interlock with the downward epidermal rete ridges. It is loose connective tissue rich in fine type I and type III collagen, oxytalan elastic fibres, fibroblasts and mast cells. The interlocking papillae resist shearing between the two layers, and capillary loops and sensory endings lie here. In sections it looks pale and loosely textured compared with the dense layer below.

The papillary dermis is the upper, finer layer of the dermis, lying directly under the epidermis and pushing up as dermal papillae into the downward epidermal ridges. Its loose matrix holds fine collagen and small elastic fibres, and capillary loops rising from the subpapillary plexus run into each papilla to nourish the epidermis, which has no blood vessels of its own. Meissner corpuscles, touch receptors that sit in these papillae of hairless skin, make this a key site for light-touch detection on the palms and soles.

The reticular dermis is the thick, deeper part of the dermis, made of dense irregular connective tissue with coarse bundles of type I collagen and thick elastic fibres. It gives the skin its tensile strength and recoil, and in the palms and soles it contains the eccrine sweat glands, the deep vascular plexus and larger nerves. The predominant direction of these bundles produces Langer's cleavage lines, and tears in the fibres form stretch marks (striae).

The reticular dermis lies beneath the papillary layer as a dense, coarse connective-tissue layer that anchors the skin to the hypodermis below. Its thick type I collagen bundles and elastic fibres are arranged in an irregular mesh, so the tissue is strong and springs back after stretching. Sweat glands, the deep vascular plexus and nerves lie within it. In sections it stains a dense, deep pink, in contrast to the looser papillary layer above.

Melanocytes are dendritic pigment cells derived from the embryonic neural crest, sitting among the basal keratinocytes at about one in every ten basal cells. Their long dendrites reach up between the spinous cells and pass melanin packets (melanosomes) to about 36 keratinocytes each, forming the epidermal melanin unit; the receiving cells then place pigment caps over their nuclei against ultraviolet light. Skin colour depends on the type and amount of melanin rather than on melanocyte number. They are best seen with a melanin stain such as Fontana-Masson.

Hypodermis septa are the fibrous connective-tissue partitions that run through the subcutaneous fat, dividing it into lobules. They are made of dense collagen bundles that extend from the underside of the dermis down to the deep fascia, anchoring the skin to the structures beneath. The larger blood vessels and nerves supplying the skin run within them. In the palms and soles the septa are thick and numerous, helping to fix the skin there firmly.

Adipose lobules are the small clusters of white fat cells that fill the hypodermis, each one partly enclosed by the fibrous septa. Each adipocyte (fat cell) holds a single large droplet of fat that pushes its nucleus to one edge, giving it a signet-ring look in sections. A fine capillary network runs through every lobule to supply these cells. The fat stores energy, insulates the body and cushions the skin.

Adipose lobules are compartments of white adipose tissue (fat-storage tissue), bounded by fibrous septa within the hypodermis. Their cells are mainly unilocular adipocytes (fat cells with one droplet) that store energy as triglyceride. Lobules are supplied by capillaries that let the fat cells exchange nutrients; in a section they look like a mosaic of pale, empty-looking cells.

The secretory coil is the coiled, blind-ending tubular part of an eccrine sweat gland, lying in the deep dermis or upper hypodermis. Its wall contains clear cells, which secrete watery primary sweat, dark cells, which add glycoprotein, and myoepithelial cells beneath them that contract to squeeze the sweat out. It is supplied by sympathetic cholinergic (acetylcholine-releasing) fibres, and the body has about two to four million eccrine glands, densest on the palms and soles. In section, look for pale clear cells and more deeply stained dark cells.

The eccrine sweat duct is the narrow tube that carries sweat from the secretory coil through the dermis, then spirals up through the epidermis (the acrosyringium) to open at a sweat pore. Its wall is two layers of small, darker cuboidal cells that reabsorb sodium and chloride through epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) and CFTR chloride channels, so the sweat reaching the surface is hypotonic (less salty than the original secretion). Cystic fibrosis, which disables CFTR, leaves sweat abnormally salty, which is the basis of the sweat test.

Arterioles are the small, muscular terminal branches of arteries that carry blood into the skin's vascular network. They run in the deep dermis and form the deep plexus, with branches rising to the subpapillary plexus beneath the papillae. Their thick smooth muscle wall, supplied by sympathetic vasoconstrictor fibres, narrows or widens the vessel to regulate blood flow and heat loss. In sections, they have a relatively thick muscular wall and a small round lumen.

Venules are the small, thin-walled vessels that collect blood from the capillaries and carry it towards the veins. In the skin they gather blood from the capillary loops and drain into the subpapillary and deep venous plexuses. Their wall is thin, with little smooth muscle and a wider lumen than the neighbouring arterioles, which helps tell them apart in a section. Venules also let white cells leave the blood during inflammation.

The subpapillary plexus is the horizontal network of small arterioles and venules lying just beneath the dermal papillae, at the junction between the papillary and reticular dermis. Its arterioles give rise to the capillary loops that enter each papilla, so it controls how much blood reaches the superficial skin. Because its vessels can dilate and constrict, the plexus plays a major part in regulating skin temperature. In a section, look for a band of vessels running parallel to the surface beneath the papillae.

Papillary capillary loops are the hairpin-shaped capillaries that rise from the subpapillary plexus into each dermal papilla. Their thin endothelial walls let oxygen and nutrients diffuse across the basement membrane into the epidermis, which has no blood vessels of its own. In a section, look for small profiles containing red blood cells at the tips of the papillae, just beneath the epidermis.

Cutaneous nerves are branches of the peripheral nerves that carry sensory and autonomic fibres to the skin. They run through the hypodermis and deep dermis as bundles of myelinated and unmyelinated axons wrapped in a tough perineurial sheath. Their sensory fibres carry touch, pain and temperature from the skin, while sympathetic fibres run to sweat glands and blood vessels. In a section, look for a rounded bundle of many small axon profiles lying among the fat or collagen.

Free nerve endings are the bare, capsule-free terminal branches of sensory axons that end between cells in the epidermis and dermis. Most are unmyelinated C fibres or thinly myelinated A-delta fibres, which detect pain, temperature and itch. Because they have no capsule, they are not visible as discrete bodies in routine stains. In silver or PGP 9.5 immunostains (a nerve marker), look for fine, beaded axons running between keratinocytes.

Meissner corpuscles are small, oval, encapsulated touch receptors that sit in the dermal papillae of hairless skin, especially the fingertips, palms and soles. Each is a stack of flattened lamellar cells (modified Schwann cells) inside a thin capsule, with a myelinated axon entering and branching between the lamellae. They are rapidly adapting, so they respond to light touch, fine texture and the start of movement across the skin. In a section, look for an ovoid structure with stacked nuclei in a papilla.

Basal keratinocytes are the youngest cells of the epidermis, forming the single row that rests on the basement membrane. They are cuboidal to columnar, with round nuclei, and they make K5 and K14 keratins that give the cell its strength. Some are stem cells that renew the epidermis, while their daughters divide a few more times before moving upward. In a section they look like a row of small, dark-nucleated cells standing on the membrane.

The stratum basale (basal layer) sits at the bottom of the epidermis, anchored to the dermis by a basement membrane. It is the main site of cell division in the epidermis, so it supplies the new keratinocytes that replace those lost from the surface. Its undersurface is shaped into rete ridges that interlock with the dermal papillae. In a section, it is the single row of dark cells along the dermal border, with melanocytes among them.

Spinous keratinocytes are the many-sided cells of the stratum spinosum, lying above the basal cells. Neighbouring cells are joined by numerous desmosomes, which look like short spines or prickles between cells in fixed tissue. Their cytoplasm contains bundles of keratin filaments (mainly K1 and K10) that strengthen the cell against mechanical stress. In sections, the polygonal outline and spiky cell borders identify them.

The stratum spinosum (spiny layer) lies between the basal layer and the granular layer, and it forms the bulk of the living epidermis. It is several cell layers deep, and its cells are linked by desmosomes that give the epidermis mechanical strength. Langerhans cells, which capture antigens and migrate to lymph nodes, are scattered within it. Acantholysis, the loss of cell-to-cell contact, occurs here in pemphigus vulgaris, an autoimmune blistering disease.

Granular cells are the flattened cells of the stratum granulosum, the layer just below the dead surface. They are packed with dark, blue-staining keratohyalin granules made of profilaggrin and loricrin, which give them a granular look in sections. Their lamellar bodies release lipid into the spaces between cells, and tight junctions form between them to complete the waterproof barrier. Their nuclei and organelles break down as they move up towards the surface.

The stratum granulosum lies between the spinous cells below and the flattened dead layer above, and is only one to five cells thick. Its cells contain keratohyalin granules, and their lipid-filled lamellar bodies build the waterproof barrier that prevents water loss. The layer is also where profilaggrin begins to be converted to filaggrin, which helps keratin filaments clump together. In a section it is a darker, purplish band just below the pale stratum corneum.

Stratum lucidum cells are flattened, dead keratinocytes that form the clear layer of thick palmar and plantar skin. They have lost their nuclei and organelles, and their cytoplasm is packed with eleidin, a translucent intermediate between keratohyalin and keratin. This makes them glassy and eosinophilic (pink-staining), so the layer stands out as a sharp, bright band above the dark granular cells.

The stratum lucidum is a thin, translucent band of the epidermis that lies just under the dead surface layer in the palms and soles. It is absent from the rest of the body's skin, so its presence in a section is a reliable sign of thick, weight-bearing skin. Its cells have lost their nuclei and are filled with eleidin, which is why the band looks glassy.

Corneocytes are the flat, dead cells of the stratum corneum, the end product of keratinisation. They have no nucleus or organelles, and their interior is packed with keratin filaments and filaggrin breakdown products that help hold water. Their outer surface is a tough cornified envelope of cross-linked protein, and neighbouring cells stay joined by corneodesmosomes until they are shed. In a section, they are flat, pale and have no nuclei.

The stratum corneum is the outer layer of the epidermis, a protective barrier that resists water loss, abrasion and micro-organisms. It is made of many layers of dead, flattened cells, and the surface cells are continuously shed by desquamation (shedding). On the palm and sole it is much thicker than elsewhere on the body, which suits the repeated pressure and friction these surfaces take.

Keratinocyte cell boundaries are the plasma membranes where neighbouring keratinocytes meet, joined by desmosomes (small adhesion junctions) that hold the epidermis together. In the living layers these junctions give the cells their spiny outline, and in the stratum corneum cornified envelopes outline the flattened dead cells. Under the electron microscope, desmosomes appear as dense plaques on either side of a narrow intercellular gap.

Keratinocyte cell boundaries are the borders between neighbouring keratinocytes, the main cells of the living epidermis, where the membranes of adjacent cells meet. Desmosomes, small anchoring junctions, join these borders and give the cells of the stratum spinosum their spiny outline, so the epidermis holds together under stress. In a section, the boundaries show as fine lines separating the polygonal cells.

Cornified cell boundaries are the outlines of the flattened, dead keratinocytes of the stratum corneum, the outermost layer of the epidermis. Each outline is a cornified envelope, a tough layer of cross-linked proteins lying under the cell membrane, and lipid-rich material fills the gaps between cells. Together, the envelope and these lipids make the surface water-resistant and wear-resistant, and in a section these cells look pink, lack nuclei and have sharp outlines.

Keratinocyte nuclei are the nuclei of the epidermal keratinocytes, the cells that make keratin and form most of the epidermis. They are round to oval and stain deep blue-violet in standard haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) sections, most clearly in the stratum basale and stratum spinosum. The nuclei shrink and fade in the upper stratum granulosum and are gone in the stratum corneum, where the cells are dead.

Keratohyalin granules are dense, blue-staining (basophilic) granules in the cells of the stratum granulosum, the granular layer just beneath the stratum corneum. They contain profilaggrin, a precursor protein that is later converted into filaggrin, which clumps keratin filaments together, and loricrin, a structural protein that helps build the cornified envelope. In haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) sections they appear as dark purple-blue clumps in the cytoplasm of these flattened cells, which helps identify the granular layer.

The melanocyte soma (cell body) and dendrites are the body and branching arms of a melanocyte, the pigment-producing cell that sits in the stratum basale among the basal keratinocytes. The dendrites extend between neighbouring keratinocytes, and the cell body often looks pale, with a clear halo around its nucleus. Melanocytes make melanin inside melanosomes (membrane-bound pigment packets) and pass these to keratinocytes, which gives the skin its colour.

The melanocyte nucleus is the nucleus of a melanocyte, the pigment-producing cell that lies in the stratum basale between basal keratinocytes. It is round or oval and usually paler-staining than the neighbouring keratinocyte nuclei, which helps to tell melanocytes apart in a section. Melanocytes arise from neural crest cells, an embryonic cell population, and transfer melanin to the surrounding keratinocytes.

Eccrine clear cells are the pale-staining secretory cells of the coil of an eccrine sweat gland, the coiled part of the gland that lies deep in the dermis. Their cytoplasm looks pale because it is rich in glycogen, a stored sugar, and they secrete the watery primary sweat, a fluid that is isotonic (has the same salt concentration) as blood plasma. They sit on the basal lamina (a thin supporting sheet) around a central lumen, with dark cells interspersed among them.

Eccrine dark cells are the darker-staining secretory cells of the coil of an eccrine sweat gland, lying alongside the clear cells. Their cytoplasm looks dark because it is packed with secretory granules containing glycoproteins (sugar-protein compounds), which are thought to add a mucus-like component to the sweat. In a section, their granular, deep-staining cytoplasm contrasts with the pale clear cells beside them.

Eccrine secretory nuclei are the nuclei of the clear and dark cells that line the secretory coil of an eccrine sweat gland. They are round and stain deep blue-violet in haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) sections, so they show as dark round dots among the pale and granular cytoplasm of the coil. The duct, by contrast, is lined by two layers of small cuboidal (cube-shaped) cells, which helps tell the two parts of the gland apart.

Myoepithelial basal profiles are the flattened, star-shaped myoepithelial cells that wrap around the secretory coil and duct of an eccrine sweat gland, lying between the secretory cells and the basal lamina (a thin supporting sheet). These cells contain actin and myosin filaments, the same contractile proteins as muscle, so when they contract they squeeze sweat out of the gland. In a section, look for their flattened, dark nuclei pressed against the outer surface of the gland.

Eccrine duct luminal cells are the inner layer of cuboidal cells that line the lumen of the eccrine sweat duct, the narrow tube that carries sweat from the coil to the skin surface. These cells reabsorb sodium and chloride as the sweat passes along the duct, which is why sweat reaching the surface is less salty than the sweat made in the coil. In a section, look for the inner ring of small cuboidal cells around a narrow lumen.

Eccrine duct basal cells form the outer layer of the wall of the eccrine sweat duct, lying on the basal lamina (a thin supporting sheet) beneath the luminal cells. They are small cuboidal cells that separate the luminal cells from the surrounding connective tissue. In a section, look for an outer ring of small cells beneath the inner luminal ring, which together make up the two-layered wall of the duct.

Eccrine duct nuclei are the nuclei of the cells that form the two-layered wall of the eccrine sweat duct, the inner luminal cells and the outer basal cells. The nuclei are round and stain deep blue-violet in haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) sections, and in cross-section they lie in two rings around a narrow central lumen. Two rings of nuclei around one small lumen are a useful clue for telling a duct apart from the secretory coil.

The Meissner capsule is the thin connective tissue sheath that encloses a Meissner corpuscle, a light-touch receptor in a dermal papilla of hairless palm and sole skin. It is continuous with the perineurium (the connective tissue sheath around a nerve bundle) of the nerve that enters the corpuscle, and it holds the stacked lamellar cells together. In a section, the capsule appears as a thin rim that separates the corpuscle from the surrounding dermal connective tissue.

Meissner lamellar cells are flattened, modified Schwann cells (the myelin-forming cells of peripheral nerves) stacked in thin, plate-like layers inside the capsule of a Meissner corpuscle. Their layers are separated by narrow spaces, and they wrap around the nerve terminal at the centre of the corpuscle. In a section, the stack of lamellar cells gives the corpuscle its layered look and helps to transmit light touch to the nerve ending.

Meissner lamellar nuclei are the flattened, elongated nuclei of the lamellar cells that make up a Meissner corpuscle. Because each lamella is a thin plate, its nucleus is stretched and lies roughly parallel to the layers, appearing as a narrow, dark streak. Recognising these streaks helps to identify the corpuscle, which lies in a dermal papilla just beneath the epidermis.

keys: Meissner entering axon and terminal cover
parts.description: The Meissner entering axon and terminal is the myelinated sensory nerve fibre that enters a Meissner corpuscle, where it loses its myelin sheath and branches into coiled, unmyelinated endings between the lamellar cells. The fibre belongs to a rapidly adapting mechanoreceptor (a touch sensor that responds to change) that detects light touch and fine texture. In a section, look for a myelinated nerve fibre entering the capsule from the dermis and losing its myelin among the lamellar cells.

Pacinian corpuscle lamellae are the concentric layers of flattened, fibroblast-like cells and collagen that surround the central nerve ending of a Pacinian corpuscle. The layers are separated by thin, fluid-filled spaces, which let the corpuscle respond mainly to rapid changes in pressure while filtering out sustained pressure. In a section they appear as concentric rings, like the layers of an onion, a pattern that identifies the corpuscle in the deep dermis and hypodermis.

The Pacinian axon terminal is the bare, unmyelinated nerve ending at the centre of a Pacinian corpuscle, enclosed by the inner core cells. The myelinated axon loses its myelin as it enters the corpuscle, and the naked terminal runs along the core's axis. It is a rapidly adapting mechanoreceptor that responds to vibration and rapid changes in pressure, and in a section it appears as a fine central strand within the onion-like lamellae.
